content:
Is there a preference regarding the use of ext1 vs. ext in Mathlib proofs in the (frequent) case that only one level of extensionality is desired and possible?

I've been tending towards ext1, on the grounds that

  • it signals to whoever is reading the proof that extensionality is applied once, not several times;
  • it should be (slightly) more efficient: the tactic does not have to check if further extensionality lemmas might be applicable after applying the first.

Apart from the (rather minor) performance question, this comes down to which of the two should be the "default", i.e. either

  • use ext unless it would do too much, in which case use ext1, or
  • use ext1 unless you want several levels of extensionality, inwhich case use ext.

The third option would be to leave the decision to the PR authors.

Any opinions?

(This came up during review of #36458; @Anne Baanen who asked me to change ext1 to ext.)
I prefer the first option - default to ext

Snir Broshi said:

I prefer the first option - default to ext

Why?

Because it's named ext, aka extensionality, which is exactly what I want to do and communicate to the reader. It's also less typing.
If in a parallel universe ext1/ext were named ext/ext* (where the star signifies repetition), I would still vote ext.

I was told at some point (by whom? I don't remember) that ext1 was an implementation detail and that we should use ext : 1 instead. It's also nice to use the same pattern ext : n for all values of n and not use something special for 1.
That looks like a better argument to me.

Michael Stoll said:

That looks like a better argument to me.

But that shifts the question to ext vs ext : 1
Then the added complexity becomes more relevant; I think I would prefer ext over ext : 1.
I personally use ext : 1 only when ext does too much work (but that does not answer the question of what we should do).
In any case, if there is a preference for Mathlib, it should be documented (in the docstring for ext/ ext1 and perhaps also in the style guide).

Rémy Degenne said:

I was told at some point (by whom? I don't remember) that ext1 was an implementation detail and that we should use ext : 1 instead. It's also nice to use the same pattern ext : n for all values of n and not use something special for 1.

It was me!

Some statistics (git grep <pattern> | wc -l in ~/mathlib4):

' ext '        : 9706
' ext$'        : 2713
' ext;'        : 2921

'ext1'         :  929
' ext1'        :  925
' ext1 '       :  520
' ext1$'       :  258
' ext1;'       :  152

'ext : 1'      :  178
'ext .* : 1'   :   93
'ext : 2'      :   44
'ext .* : 2'   :   71
'ext : 3'      :   21
'ext .* : 3'   :   43
'ext : 4'      :    3
'ext .* : 4'   :    9
'ext : 5'      :    1
'ext .* : 5'   :    1
'ext : [6-9]'  :    0
'ext .* : 6'   :    2
'ext .* [7-9]' :    0

I'm in favour of ext : 1 over ext over ext1 when all do the same thing, and ext : n where appropriate. The reason I prefer ext : n over ext is essentially for the two reasons Michael gives in the original message, plus it's more robust against new ext lemmas getting added (admittedly this isn't often, but on the general principle of "tactic calls should be stable if upstream adds a new attribute").
what does "ext : n where appropriate" mean? does that mean we should use it when we can? or not use it when we can avoid it? i should read.
does that mean that ext is a flexible tactic, and should be treated as such by the linter?
In my opinion, yes. But this may be a minority opinion.

Bhavik Mehta said:

The reason I prefer ext : n over ext is essentially for the two reasons Michael gives in the original message, plus it's more robust against new ext lemmas getting added

It's not more robust to splitting an ext lemma into a composition of two ext lemmas, which IME happens just as often as adding a new relevant ext lemma. I otherwise agree
True, but in that case IME it's easier to see what the failure is, since the goal afterwards has been under- rather than over- extd.
